https://www.laois-nationalist.ie/news/fr.text: Sun, 26 Jul, 2026 - 08:05 Fr Paddy Byrne: A family who paid the ultimate sacrifice in life Józef and Wiktoria Ulma with five of their children were a beacon of resilience, intellect, and humanity       I WAS greatly inspired recently by the story of the Ulma family, patrons of family life and the unborn child. In a world overshadowed by terror and brutality, the story of Józef and Wiktoria Ulma and their six young children shines as a beacon of humanity and moral clarity. Living in the quiet village of Markowa in southeastern Poland during the dark years of the Holocaust, the Ulmas epitomized the extraordinary courage of ordinary people. Risking everything, they sheltered eight Jewish neighbours in their modest home, defying the oppressive machinery of Nazi Germany. Their ultimate sacrifice - losing their lives and those of their children - stands as a profound testament to the power of empathy and faith in the face of unimaginable danger. Józef and Wiktoria Ulma were a beacon of resilience, intellect, and humanity. Their lives, though marked by simplicity, were extraordinary in their depth and purpose. Józef, born in 1900, was a man of immense curiosity and practical genius. He transcended his humble beginnings. His interests were vast, ranging from horticulture to photography. Wiktoria, born in 1912, was equally remarkable. Orphaned at a young age, she displayed resilience and a zest for life, attending courses at a local Folk High School and engaging in cultural activities like village theatre. Together, the Ulmas created a household filled with love, learning, and faith. Parents to six children and expecting a seventh, their lives revolved around nurturing not only their family but also their community. Before the Second World War, Markowa was a quiet, close-knit community of about 4,500 residents, including around 120 Jews. While cultural and religious differences meant that Polish and Jewish residents lived somewhat parallel lives, relations were amicable. Jewish families in Markowa primarily engaged in trade and farming, their children attending schools alongside Polish peers. Religious gatherings often took place in nearby ÅaÅcut, at a synagogue that likely welcomed the Goldman family - the very neighbours the Ulmas would later risk everything to protect. The peaceful life of the Ulmas and their neighbours shattered with the German invasion of Poland in 1939. For the Jewish community of Markowa the occupation brought swift and devastating oppression. Early restrictions, such as wearing the Star of David, escalated into forced labour, deportations, and mass executions. By 1942, ‘Operation Reinhardt’ sought to exterminate the Jewish population in the General Government area, leaving Jewish families in Markowa desperate for refuge. Markowa fell under the jurisdiction of brutal German and local collaborators. Daily life became a litany of terror: curfews, forced labour, and deportations were commonplace. The Jewish residents, targeted with relentless persecution, were subjected to confiscations, ghettos, and ultimately, extermination. The Ulmas, known for their kindness and connection to local Jewish families, did not hesitate. In December 1942, they opened their modest home to eight Jews: Saul Goldman, his four sons, two daughters, and a young child. For over a year, these individuals lived hidden within the Ulmas’ home, sharing the family’s meagre resources. Such an act of defiance carried the ultimate risk; under the German Nazi decrees, anyone aiding Jews faced immediate execution, a punishment that extended to entire households. In the early hours of March 24, 1944, German gendarmes and local collaborators arrived at the Ulma home. The brutality was swift and unrelenting. The eight Jewish individuals hiding in the house were executed immediately. Józef and Wiktoria were then dragged outside and shot. As Wiktoria fell, in the throes of childbirth, the executioners made a harrowing decision: they would kill the children too. Eight-year-old StanisÅawa, six-year-old Barbara, five-year-old WÅadysÅaw, four-year-old Franciszek, three-year-old Antoni, and 1.5-year-old Maria were all executed. In an instant, 17 lives were extinguished, including Wiktoria’s unborn child. The Ulmas were guided by an unshakable faith. Their well-worn Bible contained underlined passages from the parable of the Good Samaritan and the commandment to love one’s neighbour, reflecting the principles that shaped their actions. These were not mere ideals; they were convictions put into practice, even at the cost of their lives. Their choice to shelter Jews was an act of profound moral courage, rooted in love and a sense of shared humanity. The family’s beatification by the Catholic Church in 2023 underscores their spiritual legacy. While their recognition as Righteous Among the Nations resonates deeply within Jewish memory, their elevation to sainthood amplifies their story on a global scale, reminding Catholics and non-Catholics alike of the universal values they represent compassion, sacrifice, and unwavering moral clarity. What makes the Ulmas’ story uniquely compelling is not just the magnitude of their sacrifice but the life they led before their tragic end. Józef and Wiktoria were not wealthy, educated elites, but rather a humble couple driven by intellectual curiosity, strong faith, and a sense of communal responsibility. They cultivated their farm, raised their children, and enriched their village through Józef’s photography, ingenuity, and activism. Their decision to protect others in a time of extreme peril was not born of wealth or privilege but of an extraordinary humanity that transcended fear. The Ulma family’s story transcends national and religious boundaries. It is a testament to the enduring power of human dignity in the face of unspeakable evil. The Ulmas stand as symbols of resistance and humanity during one of history’s darkest chapters. Their legacy challenges us to reflect on our own capacity for courage and compassion. Today, as their names appear in museums, textbooks, and prayers, the Ulmas remind the world that even in the bleakest times, ordinary people can achieve extraordinary heroism. Their story is not merely one of martyrdom but a beacon of hope and a call to action for future generations. Prayer to the Ulma Family Almighty and eternal God, we thank You for the testimony of the heroic love of the spouses Józef and Wiktoria with their children, who gave their lives to save persecuted Jews. May their prayers and example support families in Christian life and help everyone to follow the true path of holiness. Lord, if it is in accordance with Your will, kindly grant me the grace … for which I am asking You through their intercession and count them among the Blessed. Through Christ our Lord. Amen. https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/s.text: Lithuanian soldiers secure the area near Pratkunai village, Kaisiadorys district, on Tuesday, where Italian fighter jets shot down a drone early on Tuesday. Photograph: Mindaugas Kulbis/AP View image in fullscreen Lithuanian soldiers secure the area near Pratkunai village, Kaisiadorys district, on Tuesday, where Italian fighter jets shot down a drone early on Tuesday. Photograph: Mindaugas Kulbis/AP Nato Russian warship fires flares at Danish helicopter as Nato jets shoot down drone over Lithuania Ursula von der Leyen says incidents ‘part of broader pattern of Russian aggression and provocation against Europe’ Jon Henley Europe correspondent Tue 15 Sep 2026 11.18 EDT First published on Mon 14 Sep 2026 23.36 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A Russian warship fired two emergency flares at a Danish helicopter in the Baltic Sea and an Italian Nato fighter jet shot down a drone carrying an explosive device over Lithuania in what the EU described as “reckless and dangerous” Russian behaviour. Poland also scrambled fighter jets “due to the activity of Russian jet-powered unmanned aerial vehicles conducting strikes on Ukrainian territory”, the day after Polish security forces retrieved a suspected Russian drone adrift in its waters. German authorities, meanwhile, were searching for more debris on Tuesday from a drone believed to have crashed on Monday near Lake Steinhude in the Hanover region, a little more than half a mile from the German Bundeswehr’s airbase in Wunstorf. The European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, said the incidents in Denmark and Lithuania were not isolated but “part of a broader pattern of Russian aggression and provocation against Europe testing our readiness and our resolve”. She added: “Russia will find our resolve only growing stronger.” The Danish prime minister, Mette Frederiksen, also condemned “reckless action from Russia towards Denmark’s military”, adding: “Russian actions are meant to intimidate and divide. They will not succeed. We will not waver.” Denmark’s armed forces said in a statement that one of its air force’s Fennec helicopters “was fired at with flares during a routine photographic operation of a Russian frigate” which was in international waters off southern Denmark. The frigate had fired “two flares towards the helicopter” on Monday, the military’s statement said. “One of the flares passed at close range to the helicopter.” View image in fullscreen From left: Gitanas Nausėda, president of Lithuania; Mette Frederiksen, the Danish prime minister, and Kristen Michal, prime minister of Estonia, at the European Arctic summit in Rovaniemi, Finland on Monday. Photograph: Jouni Porsanger/Reuters No warning or radio contact was given before the flares were fired and they came within “a matter ​of metres” of the helicopter, the Danish defence minister, Jeppe ‌Bruus, said. He said the ‌helicopter had been following standard procedures to photograph the vessel, an operation carried out “many times” in the past. The Danish foreign minister, Lars Løkke Rasmussen, said on Tuesday he had summoned the Russian ambassador over the incident. “Russia is gradually shifting the boundary for what they consider acceptable behaviour,” he said. “This is completely unacceptable and could have put human lives at risk. That is something we cannot accept,” he said. The Danish straits are the main sea route in and out ​of the Baltic Sea for commercial ​and military shipping. Russia’s ambassador to Denmark, Vladimir Barbin, said it was “not the first time” Danish helicopters had “carried out dangerous manoeuvres near Russian warships”, accusing this one of “provocative actions” against the Russian frigate. Map The Lithuanian president, Gitanas Nausėda, said early on Tuesday a drone “that just entered Lithuanian airspace was destroyed by Nato fighter jets”, adding: “With Russia intensifying its aggression against Ukraine, such readiness is vital for our region.” The drone fell near the village of Pratkūnai, about 60 miles (100km) west of the capital, Vilnius, and near the Kaunas reservoir, and had most likely entered the country’s airspace form Belarus, Lithuania’s national crisis management centre said. The centre’s head, Vilmantas Vitkauskas, told LRT public radio the drone had remained in Lithuanian airspace for about 30 minutes and had flown along the outskirts of populated areas before being intercepted. Italy’s defence minister, Guido Crosetto, said it “most probably” came from Russia and his Lithuanian counterpart, Robertas Kaunas, said an explosive device had been “discovered and subsequently neutralised” during a search of the site, near a pumped-storage hydroelectric plant. Lithuania’s foreign minister, Kęstutis Budrys, said Nato allies had been informed about the incident and discussions were under way “both in the EU and Nato, because it is obvious that we all still have a lot of homework to do”. Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia – all of which are Nato members and share a border with Russia – have regularly reported drone incursions since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. A Nato fighter shot down a Ukrainian drone over Estonia in May. European officials have said Russia has been diverting Ukrainian drones meant to strike industrial facilities and oil terminals in the St Petersburg region on the Gulf of Finland. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to This is Europe The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment after newsletter promotion View image in fullscreen Contractors work along the railway line in Holten, the Netherlands, after trains were halted. Photograph: Vincent Jannink/EPA Poland said early on Tuesday it had launched “aviation operations” in its airspace because Russian jet-powered drones were “conducting strikes on Ukrainian territory”. The operations were “preventive” and concluded without any violation of Polish airspace being observed, it later said. They came after the country’s defence minister, Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, said on Monday that the military had located ⁠and recovered a Russian drone from the Baltic Sea near the ​beach in Rusinowo, close ‌to the coastal town of Jarosławiec. Poland’s prime minister, ​Donald Tusk, has ​repeatedly said Nato countries ​should expect an increase in provocations from Moscow. A ​ Russian drone hit ‌a passenger ​train on ​Ukraine’s border with Poland on Sunday, shortly after the former British prime minister Boris Johnson and other foreign diplomats had used the same line. View image in fullscreen TV picture of a suspected Russian drone lying on a Baltic Sea beach after it was retrieved by the Polish military on Monday. Photograph: AFPTV/TVN/AFP/Getty Images In the Netherlands, train services were severely disrupted by deliberate ⁠acts of sabotage in more than 30 places around the country, the national rail infrastructure operator said, adding that it was not yet known who was responsible. The Dutch rail infrastructure operator, ProRail, said lengths of steel pipe had been “deliberately” attached to railway tracks in more than 30 locations, mainly in ⁠rural areas in the middle and the east of the country. “We are classifying this as ​sabotage of railway infrastructure,” ‌a ProRail spokesperson, Joke ‌van der Cruysen, said. All trains in the vicinity of the track blockages were halted, while there were also serious disruptions elsewhere, including to international services ‌to Germany. The ​Dutch intelligence agency, AIVD, said it was investigating the incidents, which were uncovered hours before King Willem-Alexander opened a ‌new session of parliament on Tuesday with a speech setting out the government’s 2027 budget plans. Angry farmers set hay bales and tyres alight alongside several main roads later on Tuesday, forcing authorities to ​close them and seriously affecting traffic. The militant Farmers Defence Force said it was not responsible for the railway sabotage, but could not rule out farmers taking action individually. https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.text: The autonomous vessel being deployed by the CSIRO in waters off Hobart for its months-long mission. Photograph: CSIRO View image in fullscreen The autonomous vessel being deployed by the CSIRO in waters off Hobart for its months-long mission. Photograph: CSIRO Australian climate and environmental reporting Climate crisis ‘Robust little’ vessel begins treacherous 22,000km journey around Antarctica in the name of climate science Powered by sun and wind, the uncrewed vehicle will collect data to help Australian scientists better understand how oceans absorb emissions Supported by About this content Petra Stock Fri 25 Sep 2026 11.00 EDT Last modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 11.01 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A small uncrewed vessel has embarked on a lap around Antarctica and may not return for months. The seven-metre craft, which looks like a large kayak in hi-vis orange, is expected to travel about 22,000km through inhospitable waters, propelled by powerful westerly winds and energy from the sun. The journey is seven times the distance between Sydney and Perth. Along the way, it is expected to encounter massive waves, freezing temperatures, ferocious winds, and even the odd curious seal or albatross. The mission? To collect data on carbon dioxide in the ocean and atmosphere, to help scientists better understand the role of ocean sinks. Possums in the roof, koalas in bed: study shows how animals resort to Australian homes after habitat loss Read more Dr Elizabeth Shadwick, a principal research scientist at the CSIRO, said that after leaving Hobart the vessel would travel east towards New Zealand, “eventually scooching through the Drake Passage between the bottom of South America and Antarctica, then coming along past South Africa and back to us here, where we’ll pick it up.” She hoped to see it again in seven to nine months. View image in fullscreen The vessel has a heavy keel to keep it upright and a solar sail to power it. Photograph: CSIRO AAPP The autonomous vehicle made by the US maritime company Saildrone was designed to withstand the intrepid voyage, with a heavy keel keeping it upright, a rudder to steer and a fixed solar sail poking above the surface. It would be remotely monitored by the company, who would check in regularly via satellite, and, if necessary, nudge it in the right direction. “It’s already been bashed around pretty heavily,” Shadwick said. “It’s quite a robust little device. We saw some eight metres of waves just the day after we deployed it and a 35-knot wind.” Measurements taken throughout its journey – including wind speed, atmospheric pressure, solar radiation, ocean temperature, salinity and chlorophyll, as well as carbon dioxide levels in the water and air – were expected to assist scientists in better understanding the role that oceans play in global heating . “The ocean is doing all of us a great service by absorbing about a third of anthropogenic or human emissions every year,” Shadwick said, and the Southern Ocean, around Antarctica, played a significant role. “If we want to continue to rely on this ocean service of absorbing our human emissions, we need to understand how it might change in the future.” Crewed research vessels that travelled between Hobart and Antarctica traversed only a limited patch of the ocean, she said. The autonomous craft would gather data over a greater distance and time, including crucial measurements during the polar winter. The vessel is the first in a fleet of four. Others are planned to be launched at three-monthly intervals. They will be spread across the Southern, Pacific, Atlantic and Indian oceans, particularly during winter. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | When he publishes Sign up to Clear Air Australia Adam Morton brings you incisive analysis about the politics and impact of the climate crisis after newsletter promotion View image in fullscreen The approximate route the vessel will travel to circumnavigate Antarctica. Photograph: CSIRO The scientists will be able to access information in near real time via a mission portal, and once the vessels return to home base, all data and observations will undergo quality checks before they are made available for further research. Dr Pep Canadell, a chief research scientist at the CSIRO, said for every tonne of carbon dioxide released by burning fossil fuels, about 500kg were removed by ocean and forest sinks. “This is like a 50% discount on climate change,” he said. But the amount absorbed by the oceans could change due to multiple drivers: warming waters, westerly winds, melting ice, ocean acidification and the hole in the ozone layer. Observations would enable scientists to more accurately model these processes and understand how they could change in the future, he said. Solar and wind generation meet record 80% of power demand on Australia’s national grid Read more The University of New South Wales professor Matthew England, who studies the role of ocean circulation in global climate but was not involved in the research project, said measuring how much the oceans absorbed and how that was changing was critical. “We’ve obviously got a surge of emissions going into our atmosphere. Both the terrestrial vegetation on land and the oceans absorb a big chunk of that,” he said. “We need to track that carbon uptake and understand exactly how big the absorption is. If it starts to decline in a significant way, then it tells us that we have an even bigger problem of carbon emission reductions.” The Southern Ocean was “inhospitable” with huge swells, gale force winds, sea ice and storms. “These are very tough measuring conditions for a research vessel.” So gathering data using an autonomous vehicle, without burning fuel, was “an incredible deployment of technology”, he said. https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text: August Hanning, pictured in 2006, was head of Germany’s foreign intelligence service from 1998 to 2005. Photograph: Fabrizio Bensch/Reuters View image in fullscreen August Hanning, pictured in 2006, was head of Germany’s foreign intelligence service from 1998 to 2005. Photograph: Fabrizio Bensch/Reuters Germany German court orders detention of former intelligence chief after spying arrest August Hanning, 80, appears before judge after being accused of treason and espionage on behalf of foreign state Kate Connolly in Berlin Wed 7 Oct 2026 13.03 EDT Last modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 16.01 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A formal arrest warrant has been issued against Germany’s former top spy, with a judge ordering him to be held in pre-trial detention, a day after he was arrested on suspicion of treason and spying on behalf of an overseas intelligence agency. August Hanning, 80, is accused of buying secret documents from a former colleague and using them to advise a foreign intelligence service, according to the office of the federal prosecutor. Hanning’s arrest on Tuesday , along with that of his former office head, referred to as Manfred D. It has sent shock waves through Germany’s political and intelligence community, with analysts calling it potentially the country’s biggest espionage scandal since the end of the cold war. It has raised questions in Berlin over how Germany’s foreign intelligence service can uphold its reputation internationally, particularly at a time of heightened security concerns. Also under scrutiny is the sustainability of rules governing the conduct of retired senior officials and their ability to earn extra income based on their insider knowledge and professional networks. Hanning was head of Germany’s foreign intelligence service (BND) between 1998 and 2005. A lawyer for Hanning denied he had been involved in any wrongdoing on Wednesday, telling the conservative daily newspaper Die Welt: “While it is true that he ‌was in possession of confidential documents, the allegation that he passed on information contained therein to the detriment of Germany, let alone for payment, is incorrect.” Manfred D, who was also placed under formal arrest on Wednesday by the judge in Karlsruhe, has yet to respond to questions via his lawyer. Hanning is alleged to have agreed in 2010 to pay for information from Manfred D, who allegedly then smuggled it out of the BND. Manfred D, 64, had worked under Hanning and went on to serve subsequent BND bosses after Hanning, before retiring in March this year. View image in fullscreen Members of the media attempt to take a photograph of Hanning as he is driven away from court on Wednesday. Photograph: Anna Szilágyi/EPA Hanning is believed to have received about 2,000 documents from Manfred D until June 2022, some of which were classified, according to prosecutors. He is alleged to have used the information in his papers for his private consulting work. Prosecutors were alerted to Hanning’s alleged criminal activities by investigators gathering evidence in a separate child kidnapping case involving a steakhouse restaurant dynasty, which the former spy chief is accused of participating in using his former contacts with Israeli intelligence. Christina Block, an heiress to the business, allegedly paid Hanning and a retired police officer more than €100,000 (£85,000) for their roles in the alleged abduction of her two children from her ex-husband. A report in Der Spiegel on Wednesday said investigators were looking into a possible connection to the foreign intelligence service of Azerbaijan as one of the agencies Hanning may have been passing information to. Azerbaijan’s media and broadcasting council denied any connection to Hanning or the investigation. “The malicious intent of the forces behind this disinformation operation is to damage Azerbaijan-Germany relations,” the council said in a statement. The scandal has awakened memories of the Günter Guillaume affair , when an East German Stasi spy and his wife posing as refugees infiltrated the government of the then chancellor Willy Brandt, leading to Brandt’s resignation in 1974. Marc Henrichmann, the head of the parliamentary committee overseeing the intelligence services, which has repeatedly raised questions about the post-career consulting activities of intelligence agency employees but has been told legal obstacles stood in the way of challenging them, said he was “fairly flabbergasted” by the affair, but stressed it was as yet unclear the breadth and extent of the alleged wrongdoing. “As yet we don’t know exactly what happened,” he told the public broadcaster Deutschlandfunk, while acknowledging the need to “restore broken trust” in the BND. View image in fullscreen Police officers stand outside Hanning’s home in Nordwalde on Tuesday after his arrest. Photograph: Christoph Reichwein/DPA/AP On Wednesday, politicians and intelligence analysts called for stricter regulation around allowing former security employees to make use of their influence and knowledge after retiring. The scandal comes at a time when Germany is attempting to make its intelligence agencies, including the BND and its domestic sibling, the BfV, more robust, efficient and independent from those of its allies, in particular boosting their powers of surveillance to more effectively tackle sabotage and hacking attacks, amid rising threats from external powers such as Russia and Iran. The scandal is yet another blow to the BND’s reputation. Not only is it notoriously dependent on information from foreign agencies to foil terror attacks on German soil, but it has faced other cases of its staff allegedly spying for other countries. It has also been reeling from the case of a department head, Carsten L, who was accused in December 2022 of spying for Russia. His trial is now being heard by Berlin’s higher regional court. Sensitivities over the country’s past, when dictatorships misused their powers of surveillance to spy on their own people, have made reform of the agencies hard to pursue. Hanning, the son of a brickyard owner, rose through the ranks of the intelligence service to become its head. After the attacks of 11 September 2001, he oversaw the investigation into some of the terrorists who had studied in Hamburg. He initiated wide-reaching reforms of the BND including bringing it closer to politics, becoming a close adviser to the then interior minister Wolfgang Schäuble. He spoke out against a “culture of leaks” and was deeply critical of the NSA whistleblower Edward Snowden , calling him an “internal offender”. Once his civil service career was over, Hanning continued to hold a role as a respected behind-the-scenes negotiator, and frequently intervened in government security policy debates. At the same time he built up his consultant business, founding an agency with his wife, Ruth, called Hanning Consult, and worked for various other global consulting agencies. He even produced a “spy cookbook” with his wife, called “Top(f) Secret” ( Topf being the German word for saucepan).
